questions.explanation: A caldera is much larger than a crater. A crater is formed by the outward explosion of rocks, while a caldera is a massive sinkhole formed by the inward collapse of a volcano's structural support (its magma chamber) after a massive eruption (e.g., Yellowstone Caldera).

questions.stem: Which type of volcano is characterised by broad, gently sloping flanks built by repeated eruptions of low-viscosity, fluid basaltic lava?

options.option_text: Stratovolcano, built from alternating layers of lava and ash
Shield volcano, exemplified by Mauna Loa in Hawaii
Cinder cone, formed from pyroclastic fragments and volcanic cinders
Lava dome, created by viscous silica-rich magma pooling near the vent

questions.explanation: Shield volcanoes like Mauna Loa (Hawaii) are built by low-viscosity basaltic lava that flows easily over great distances, creating wide, gently sloping structures resembling a warrior's shield laid flat. Stratovolcanoes (the most tempting distractor) have steep, conical profiles formed by alternating layers of ash and viscous lava — the exact opposite of the gently sloping form described in the stem.

questions.stem: The point within the Earth's interior where seismic energy is first released and an earthquake actually originates is termed the?

options.option_text: Epicentre, the surface point directly above the earthquake's origin
Seismic node, a junction point of multiple converging active fault lines
Hypocentre (Focus), the true underground origin point of an earthquake
Isoseismal centre, the subsurface zone recording maximum shaking intensity

questions.explanation: The hypocentre (also called focus) is the actual point below the Earth's surface where the earthquake rupture initiates and seismic energy is first released. The epicentre (the most common confusion) is not the origin — it is merely the point on the Earth's surface vertically above the hypocentre. Seismic waves radiate outward from the hypocentre in all directions.

questions.stem: The Hawaiian Islands formed progressively over millions of years as the Pacific Plate drifted over a stationary deep-mantle heat source, creating a chain of progressively older islands. What is this volcanic mechanism called?

options.option_text: Subduction-zone volcanism at a convergent tectonic plate boundary
Rift-zone volcanism along a diverging mid-ocean spreading ridge
Hot-spot volcanism driven by a fixed deep-mantle plume beneath the plate
Collision-zone volcanism from compressional continental plate tectonics

questions.explanation: Hot-spot volcanism occurs when a stationary mantle plume melts through the overlying drifting lithospheric plate. As the Pacific Plate moves north-west, older islands migrate away from the plume and become extinct, while new islands form above the hot-spot — explaining why the north-western Hawaiian islands are geologically older. Subduction-zone and mid-ocean ridge volcanism (the tempting distractors) are plate-boundary processes, whereas Hawaii is an intra-plate phenomenon.

questions.stem: On seismological intensity maps, lines drawn to connect all localities that experienced identical levels of ground shaking from the same earthquake are called?

options.option_text: Isobars, connecting points of equal atmospheric pressure variation
Isoseismal lines, linking areas of equal earthquake intensity on a map
Isochrons, marking zones of equal seismic wave arrival time delay
Seismic contours, tracing depths of equal hypocentre concentration zones

questions.explanation: Isoseismal lines connect points that experienced the same intensity (not magnitude) of earthquake shaking, measured on scales like the Modified Mercalli Intensity (MMI) scale. They form closed concentric curves around the epicentre, with innermost lines indicating maximum intensity. Isobars (the most familiar prefix for candidates) connect equal atmospheric pressure in meteorology, not seismic intensity — a common confusion due to the similar 'iso-' prefix.

questions.stem: Which type of seismic surface wave causes ground particles to move in an elliptical retrograde motion — analogous to rolling ocean waves — producing both vertical and forward-backward horizontal displacement?

options.option_text: Love waves, vibrating horizontally and perpendicular to the direction of propagation
Primary (P) waves, compressional body waves traveling through solid and liquid media
Rayleigh waves, formed by interaction of P and S waves at the Earth's free surface
Secondary (S) waves, transverse body waves that cannot propagate through liquid layers

questions.explanation: Rayleigh waves produce elliptical retrograde particle motion in the vertical plane containing the wave direction — resembling a backward-rolling ocean wave with both vertical and horizontal (forward-back) displacement. Love waves (the most tempting distractor) are also surface waves but vibrate horizontally and perpendicular to wave travel, with no vertical component whatsoever. Both surface wave types are slower than body waves (P and S) but cause the most structural damage during earthquakes.

questions.stem: The 'P-wave shadow zone', observed at angular distances of approximately 103° to 142° from an earthquake's epicentre, is primarily attributed to which property of Earth's deep interior?

options.option_text: Total reflection of P-waves at the Mohorovičić discontinuity (Moho) boundary
Progressive absorption of P-wave energy within the ductile asthenosphere layer
Refraction and inward bending of P-waves while traversing the liquid outer core
Destructive wave interference between direct P-waves and reflected PcP phases

questions.explanation: P-waves entering the Earth's liquid outer core undergo sharp refraction — bending inward due to a sudden change in density and seismic velocity at the core-mantle boundary. This deflects the waves away from the 103°–142° angular band, creating a zone where no direct P-waves arrive. The Moho (the most tempting distractor) is the crust-mantle discontinuity at a shallow depth of ~30–70 km — far too shallow to deflect waves over such large angular distances from the epicentre.

questions.stem: In volcanology, the hazardous secondary phenomenon termed 'lahar' caused catastrophic destruction in the years following the 1991 eruption of Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines. A lahar is best defined as?

options.option_text: A fast-moving cloud of superheated gas mixed with pyroclastic fragments (nuée ardente)
A volcanic mudflow or debris flow of pyroclastic material mixed with water or melted ice
A lava tube collapse creating ground fissures and releasing secondary vent emissions
A sudden phreatic explosion driven by magmatic gas pressure exceeding cap-rock strength

questions.explanation: A lahar is a volcanic mudflow — a rapidly flowing slurry of water, volcanic ash, and rocky debris channelled down river valleys around a volcano. After the 1991 Pinatubo eruption, monsoon rains remobilised vast ash deposits for years, generating lahars that buried entire towns under metres of debris. Nuée ardente (the most tempting distractor) is a pyroclastic flow — a fast-moving current of hot gas and incandescent volcanic fragments — a thermally violent but distinct phenomenon from the water-saturated lahar.
